en: *Commentary on the Awakening of Faith*, Fascicle One, composed by Wonhyo.

Regarding the *Commentary on the Awakening of Faith*, there are briefly three gates for its exposition: first, indicating the essential body (*dharmakāya*); second, explaining the title; and third... [text continues].
The third person clarifies the meaning based on the text.
First, regarding the designation of the essence of the school:
Now, as for the essence of the Mahāyāna—
Utterly empty and still;
profoundly serene and mysterious.
It is the mystery within mystery.
How could it transcend the realm of myriad phenomena?
Though it is the stillness of stillness, it remains within the discourse of the hundred schools.
It is not something that can be represented by images, for even the five eyes cannot see its form.
It lies beyond words, for even the four types of eloquence cannot describe its appearance.
If one wishes to speak of it, one must say it is vast.
Entering the innerless, nothing is omitted;
wishing to describe it as subtle,
it encompasses the outerless and yet remains in surplus.
To lead it toward existence is as empty as its application;
to obtain it within non-existence is likewise so.
All things arise by riding upon it;
one does not know how to speak of it,
so it is forcibly designated as "Mahāyāna" (the Great Vehicle).
Were it not for the great being who has sealed his mouth and the man of realization who perceives through direct insight,
who could discourse upon the Mahāyāna beyond words?
How can one give rise to profound faith in that which transcends all thought?
This is why the Bodhisattva Aśvaghoṣa, through his unconditioned great compassion, [taught thus].
It laments how the delusive winds of ignorance wound that [mind],
causing the ocean of the mind to be easily tossed about;
it takes pity on this true nature of original enlightenment.
Sleeping long in dreams, it is difficult to awaken.

Thus, one possessing the power of wisdom that realizes the identity of all things is capable of composing this treatise to extol and expound the profound and esoteric meanings of the Tathāgata’s deep sutras.
I wish to cause those who study to briefly open a single scroll and thoroughly explore the purport of the Tripiṭaka;
and to cause those who practice the Way to forever bring all phenomena to rest.
Thus, one returns to the source of the single mind.
Although what has been described is extensive,
it may be summarized as follows.
Opening two gates within a single mind,
it comprehensively summarizes the extensive teachings on the hundred and eight māras,
demonstrating the purity of nature amidst the defilement of phenomena.
He universally mastered the profound subtleties of the fifteen regions beyond the Yūsha Mountains;
such as the single flavor of the Hārītī Grove and the non-dual intent of Vulture Peak.
It is the ultimate fruit of the three bodies, identical in nature to the Golden Drum;
the profound cause of the four stages of the *Avataṃsaka-mālā*;
and the most expansive supreme path of the *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā* and the *Mahāsaṃnipāta*.
The profound and subtle gateway of the Sun-Treasury and Moon-Treasury;
the very core and essence of all such scriptures—
this is that which unifies them all as one.
Is it not this treatise alone?
Therefore, the text below states:
"It is for the purpose of comprehensively encompassing the boundless meanings of the Tathāgata’s vast and profound Dharma."
This treatise should now be explained.
Since the purport of this treatise is as such,
[it shall be set forth].
When opened, the principle of immeasurable and boundless meaning constitutes the core;
when closed, the dharma of the two gates within one mind constitutes the essential.
Within these two gates:
It accommodates ten thousand meanings without confusion;
boundless meanings are unified within a single mind in harmonious fusion.
Therefore, they exercise mastery over opening and closing,
and are unimpeded in establishing and refuting; though they open up [the teaching], they do so without prolixity.
It unites without being narrow;
it stands without anything gained;
it breaks without anything lost.
This constitutes the sublime method of Aśvaghoṣa and the essential substance of the *Śraddhotpāda-śāstra*. Nevertheless,
because the purport of this treatise is profound, those who have commented upon it in the past have rarely fully grasped its core tenets.
This is simply because each person adheres to their own habitual studies and clings to the literal phrasing,
unable to maintain an open mind in seeking the underlying meaning;
thus, they do not approach the intent of the Master of the Treatise.
Some look toward the source while losing sight of the current;
some grasp the leaves while neglecting the trunk;
some cut from the collar to patch the sleeves.
Some [commentaries] prune the branches while retaining the roots;
for now, I shall rely directly upon this treatise,
which corresponds to the specific scriptural text under discussion.
I hope that those of like inclination will examine this further. The exposition of the fundamental principle and its essence is concluded.
Next, the title of the work shall be explained.
Regarding the term "Mahāyāna":
"Great" (mahā) is the name for this Dharma;
its meaning is that of being vast and all-encompassing.
"Vehicle" (*yāna*) is a metaphorical designation;
its function is that of transport. Although this is the general explanation, [the specific details follow].
Regarding the analysis therein, there are two sections:
first, an exposition based on the sūtras;
second, an elucidation based on the śāstras.
Regarding what is taught in the sūtras,
as stated in the *Gaganagañja-sūtra*:
"The Mahāyāna..."
This means that because it is immeasurable, boundless,
and without limit, it pervades all things universally, like space.
Because it extensively accommodates all sentient beings and is not shared with śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas,
it is called the Mahāyāna.
Furthermore, as for the vehicle:
it takes the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*) practiced with correct abiding as its wheels,
and the ten wholesome courses of action (*daśakuśalakarmapatha*) thoroughly purified as its spokes.
It takes the accumulation of pure merit as its hub;
it takes firm, sincere, and single-minded concentration as its linchpins, felloes, nails, and pins;
and it takes the successful accomplishment of the various dhyānas and liberations as its shafts.
One takes the four immeasurables as the means of excellent training,
the spiritual friend as the charioteer,
and the knowledge of the timely and the untimely as the impetus for setting forth.
They use the sounds of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self as their whip;
they use the jeweled ropes of the seven factors of enlightenment as the breast-straps;
and they use the pure five eyes as their girth-bands.
It takes great compassion, vast, universal, and upright, as its streamer and banner;
it takes the four right efforts as its linchpins, axles, branches, hubs, and wheels; and it takes the four foundations of mindfulness as its level and straight alignment.
One takes the four bases of psychic power as swift advancement;
one takes the five superior powers as scouting the enemy lines;
and one takes the eightfold noble path as a direct advance.
The unobstructed wisdom-illumination regarding all sentient beings serves as its portico;
by means of the non-abiding six pāramitās, one dedicates [merit] toward *samyak-saṃprajanya*;
and by means of the unimpeded four noble truths, one crosses over to the other shore.
"This is the Mahāyāna.
The commentary explains:
The preceding twenty phrases have employed metaphors to illustrate the Dharma in order to reveal the meaning of the Vehicle (yāna).
Furthermore, the text below states:
"This vehicle is that which is received by all Buddhas and contemplated by Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas."
It is the vehicle upon which all bodhisattvas ride;
it is that which should be reverently saluted by Śakra, Brahmā, and the World-Protectors;
and it is that which should be venerated by all sentient beings.
It is worthy of praise by all those who possess omniscience;
it is the refuge to which all the world should turn;
and it cannot be destroyed by any māras.
No heterodox teachers can fathom it;
no one in the world can rival it.
The commentary explains:
The preceding ten phrases have elucidated the Mahāyāna in relation to persons.
According to the treatise, there are seven [points] based on three [categories],
which constitute the three kinds of greatness.
This will be explained below.
Regarding the phrase "seven kinds," there are two types of sevenfold sets.
First, as stated in the Abhidharma-śāstra:
"It is called the Mahāyāna because it is endowed with seven kinds of greatness."
What are the seven? First is the greatness of the object (*ālambana-mahattva*).
This is because the path of the bodhisattva takes as its object the vast teachings of immeasurable sūtras, numbering in the hundreds of thousands and so forth.
Second is the greatness of practice,
because it correctly practices all vast deeds for one's own benefit and the benefit of others.
Third is the greatness of wisdom.
Fourth is the greatness of diligence, because one understands the selflessness of persons and phenomena on a vast scale,
and because one diligently cultivates immeasurable difficult practices through skillful means for three great incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*).
Fifth is the greatness of skill in means (*upāyakauśalya*),
because of not abiding in either saṃsāra or nirvāṇa.
Sixth is the greatness of realization (*prāpti*).

Because one attains the Tathāgata’s various powers (*bala*), fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*), and uncommon Buddha-qualities (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*), as well as immeasurable and innumerable great merits.
Seventh is the greatness of activity (*karmamahattva*):

because until the very limit of *saṃsāra*, one manifests all the vast deeds of the Buddhas, such as establishing the attainment of enlightenment (*bodhi*). Among these, the first five are causes and the latter two are results. Second, the *Vyākhyāyukti* (Explication of the Manifestation) states:
The nature of the Mahāyāna refers to the Bodhisattvayāna being in common correspondence with the seven great natures.
It is called the Mahāyāna. What are the seven?
First, the greatness of the Dharma.
This refers to the vast teachings on skillful means contained within the Bodhisattva-piṭaka among the twelve divisions of the Buddha's teaching.
Second is the greatness of the arousal of the mind,
which refers to having already aroused the mind for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Third is the greatness of resolute conviction (*adhimukti*),
which refers to the arising of firm faith and understanding regarding the aforementioned objects of the greatness of the Dharma.
Fourth is the greatness of intention (*āśaya*).
This refers to having already transcended the stage of practice through resolute belief and entered the stage of pure superior intention;
it is the greatness of the five provisions.
Because they have accomplished the two great provisions of merit and wisdom,
they are able to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
This is the greatness of the six periods.
This refers to the fact that one can realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment over the course of three great *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas.
Seventh is the perfection of the nature [of enlightenment],
which refers to the very essence of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment— the perfected essence of enlightenment itself.
Compared to others, even his fully perfected selfhood has no equal,
let alone anything superior;
this is *yoga*.
The *Bodhisattvabhūmi* all states this in the same way.
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* says:
Among these, there are six kinds:
from the greatness of phenomena up to the greatness of time.
All of these are the causes for the perfect realization of the great nature;
this perfect realization of the great nature is the fruit of the six aforementioned types of great nature.
The commentary states:
Although these two types of sevenfold greatness are identical in number, [they differ in their nature].
The establishment of the distinct meanings:
the intention behind this establishment can be understood by investigating it.
The explanation of the Mahāyāna is concluded.
As for the term "Arousing Faith," it is based on this treatise.
It gives rise to faith in sentient beings;
therefore, it is called "giving rise to faith.
Faith is defined by the expression of certainty, meaning "it is thus."
That is to say: one has faith that the principle truly exists;
one has faith that it can be attained through cultivation; and one has faith that when it is attained through cultivation, there are infinite virtues.
In this context, that which truly exists through faith is the greatness of the essence of faith,
because all dharmas are found to be unattainable.
To believe that the equal dharma-realm truly exists,
and to believe that it can be attained— this is the greatness of the characteristic of faith.
Because the nature-endowed merits permeate sentient beings,
those who possess the permeation of the aspect of faith will certainly return to the source.
This is because faith possesses inexhaustible merit and function.
This faith is great; for there is nothing one will not do because of it.
If a person can give rise to these three kinds of faith, [they shall attain liberation].
One is able to enter the Buddha-dharma,
give rise to all merits,
and emerge from the realms of Māra.
One reaches the unsurpassed path.
As a verse in the sutra says:
"Faith is the source of the path and the mother of all virtues."
Increasing all roots of goodness,
eliminating all doubts and delusions,
and manifesting and opening up the unsurpassed path.
Faith can transcend all realms of Māra and manifest the unsurpassed path of liberation;
it is the indestructible seed of all meritorious virtues.
Born from the unsurpassed Bodhi tree,
one believes in such immeasurable merits; relying on the treatise,
one gives rise to the resolve for enlightenment.
Therefore, it is called "Arousing Faith.
What is meant by "treatise" (śāstra) refers to the established, definitive, and authoritative written words.
It is called a "treatise" (śāstra) because it judges and explains the principles of the profound characteristics of phenomena based on the meaning of definitive resolution.
In summary, the Mahāyāna is the fundamental essence of this treatise,
while the *Awakening of Faith* is its supreme capacity.
The essence and its function are presented together as the title; therefore,
it is called the *Mahāyāna-śraddhotpāda-śāstra* (Treatise on the Awakening of Faith in the Mahāyāna).
Third, the explanation of the text.
The text consists of three parts.
The first three lines of verse are as follows:
The section beginning with "Homage and Statement of Intent" and continuing with "The Treatise says" below constitutes the formal establishment of the body of the treatise.
The final verse summarizes the dedication.
Within the first three stanzas:
There are two intentions here:
the first two verses properly take refuge in the Triple Gem.
The final verse describes the purpose of composing this treatise.
Within the initial section on taking refuge and paying homage, there are two parts.
The two characters "take refuge" (*namas*) constitute the characteristic of that which takes refuge.
From "Throughout the ten directions" below...
To manifest the virtue that is the object of refuge:
the characteristic of that which is capable of taking refuge is the meaning of "refuge," defined as the sense of reverent compliance.
The meaning of "tending toward" (*gati*) is the meaning of "returning.
"Life" (*jīvita*) refers to the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*),
which governs all the faculties collectively.
Of all that constitutes a single body,
life alone is the master;
it is what all living beings value most.
Let nothing take precedence over this:
lift up this non-dual mandate to serve the Unsurpassed Honored One.
This expresses the ultimate limit of faith;
therefore, it is called "taking refuge.
Furthermore, "taking refuge" carries the meaning of returning to the source.
This is because the six sense faculties of sentient beings arise from a single mind.
Yet they turn their backs on their own origin and rush toward the six sense-objects;
now, by taking up the vital breath, one comprehensively gathers the six faculties.
Returning to its source, the origin of the single mind;
therefore it is called "taking refuge.
That which is returned to is the single mind.
This is because they are the Three Jewels.
From "Throughout the ten directions" onwards,
the virtues of that which is taken as refuge are revealed.
The meaning of the Three Jewels should be explained herein;
the meaning has been explained elsewhere.
For now, let us simply interpret the text.
Within the text there are three [sections], namely: Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha.
Within the Jewels (ratna) themselves, there are likewise three meanings.
First, he praises the virtue of his mind;
next, he praises the virtue of his form;
the third phrase cites the person to conclude the praise.
Within the praise of the virtues of the mind,
both its function and its essence are praised.
First, regarding the phrase "the most supreme activity throughout the ten directions":
This praises the function of karma;
that is to say, the activity of manifesting the eight signs and so forth to transform sentient beings throughout the entirety of the ten directions.
Pervading the limits of the three periods of time,
they perform all the works of a Buddha according to those who may be transformed.
Therefore, it is said that [this] is the most supreme activity throughout the ten directions.
As the Abhidharma-śāstra states:
"The greatness of karma is as follows:"
Reaching to the limit of the cycle of birth and death,
he manifests all acts such as attaining enlightenment,
thereby establishing the vast activities of all Buddhas.
That [term] refers to the three periods of time;
this [term] reveals the ten directions.
As for the term "omniscient" (sarvajña):
This praises the essence of wisdom.
The reason its functional activity pervades the ten directions is that the essence of wisdom is omnipresent.
The essence of wisdom is all-pervasive;
therefore, it is called "omniscience" (sarvajñā).
As the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states:
It is like space:
it pervades the limits of all form and is without arising, abiding, ceasing, or transformation.
The wisdom of the Tathāgata is likewise:
it pervades all that can be known,
for it is non-erroneous and immutable.
The praise of the virtues of the mind is concluded.
Next is the praise of the virtues of the form.
Within this, there are also two parts.
"Form is unimpeded" praises the subtle excellence of the essence of form;
"mastery" refers to its sovereign power.
This praises the excellence of the substance of form.
The initial mention of "the substance of form" refers to the Tathāgata’s form-body (rūpakāya).
It is accomplished through the myriad practices and accomplished through inconceivable perfuming;
although it possesses wondrous form, [it is not perceived].
And yet they are without obstruction;
each mark and each excellence is boundless and limitless.
Therefore, it is said that form is unimpeded.
As the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states:
"One might still be able to find the limit of space."
A single pore of the Buddha is without limit;
the Buddha’s virtues are thus inconceivable.
This is called the Tathāgata’s pure knowledge and vision; therefore, although he is without material obstruction, [he remains so].
Yet, because there is the meaning of manifesting through skillful means,
it is called "name-and-form" while remaining unimpeded.
As for the term "sovereign":
He praises its functions and applications,
namely, the mutual functioning of the five sense organs and the reciprocal activities of the ten bodies.
Therefore, it is said that form is sovereign.
As for the mutual functioning of the five sense organs,
this is as explained in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* among the eight masteries (*aṣṭavaśitā*).
Regarding the "creator of the ten bodily marks," as described in the "Ten Stages" chapter of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*,
this concludes the praise of the qualities of his physical form.
"The World-Savior of Great Compassion" constitutes the third phrase,
which identifies the person and offers a concluding eulogy.
The Buddha is like a great elder.
Taking sentient beings as his children,
he enters the burning house of the triple world to rescue them from the suffering of being consumed by flames.
Therefore, it is said that he "saves the world.
The virtue of saving the world is precisely great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).
Compassion that is free from [the distinction between] self and other, which is compassion without an object,
is the most excellent among all forms of compassion.
Therefore, it is called "Great Compassion.
Among all the myriad virtues possessed within the stage of Buddhahood,
the Tathāgata employs Great Compassion alone as his power.
Therefore, I have cited them selectively to manifest the person of the Buddha,
as stated in the *Ekottarika Āgama*:
The powers of ordinary beings and sages are of six kinds. What are these six?
Infants take crying as their power.
If one wishes to say something,
one must first weep;
for women take anger as their strength.
Based on this aversion,
it was subsequently stated that śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas take patience as their strength.
One should always consider oneself inferior to others before speaking of oneself;
for kings take pride and arrogance as their strength.
He speaks of himself by means of this noble power;
the Arhat speaks of himself by means of the power of single-minded application.
The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, take great compassion as their power because they extensively benefit sentient beings; thus,
it is known that the Buddhas specifically take great compassion as their power.
Therefore, to manifest the name "Great Compassionate One," the three preceding phrases have concluded the praise of the Buddha Jewel;
the following two phrases [are now presented].
Next, to reveal the Jewel of the Dharma and its bodily characteristics:
this refers to the body of the Tathāgata as previously described.
This refers to the Reward Buddha (*vipākabuddha*).
Since he takes the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) as his very essence,
it is said to be the essential characteristic of that body.
This refers to citing the Buddha to take up his Dharma.
The following phrase correctly sets forth the essential characteristics of the Jewel of the Dharma.
As for the term "dharma-nature" (dharmatā):
That which is called nirvāṇa is the fundamental nature of phenomena; therefore,
it is named "dharma-nature" (dharmatā).
As stated in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*:
"Dharma" refers to nirvāṇa, the state free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*);
"nature" (*prakṛti*) refers to the fundamental seeds.
Just as yellow stone has the nature of gold and white stone has the nature of silver,
so too do all phenomena possess the nature of nirvāṇa.
Therefore, it is called the "dharma-nature" (*dharmatā*).
As for what is called "true thusness" (*tathatā*): it is termed "true" (*tathā*) because it is without anything to be discarded.
That which has no establishment is called "suchness" (*tathatā*). As stated in the subsequent passage:
"The essence of this true suchness is such that there is nothing to be discarded."
Because all phenomena are entirely true,
there is nothing that can be established.
Because all phenomena are identical to suchness.
One should know that all phenomena are ineffable and inconceivable;
therefore, they are called "Suchness" (Tathatā).
As for what is called the "ocean":
To illustrate the Dharma through a metaphor,
it shall be explained briefly:
the ocean possesses four meanings.
First, it is profoundly deep;
second, it is vast and expansive;
third, its hundred jewels are inexhaustible.
Fourth, the myriad images appear as reflections;
one should know that the great ocean of true thusness is likewise,
for it forever severs the hundred negations.
Because it enwraps and contains all things;
because there is no virtue that is not complete within it;
and because there is no form that does not manifest therein.
Therefore, it is called the ocean of the *dharmatā-tathatā*.
As the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says:
"For example, like the deep great ocean."
The precious jewels are inexhaustible;
within them, the various forms and likenesses of all sentient beings are fully manifested.
The ocean of profound causes and conditions contains inexhaustible jewels of merit within the pure dharmakāya.
Because it is formless and does not manifest.
This concludes the praise of the Dharma Jewel.
The following two phrases are as follows:
He praises the Jewel of the Sangha;
by speaking of it as a "repository of immeasurable merit," he cites its virtues to extol the person.
This refers to bodhisattvas on the stages who,
by practicing a single course of conduct,
integrate all ten thousand practices.
Each and every one of these lines is equal to the Dharma-realm,
being without limit or measure;
they are obtained through the accumulation of merit.
For this reason, it is said that there are immeasurable merits.
Such merits belong entirely to the bodhisattva.
Because a person can gather virtuous qualities,
it is called a "treasury" (kośa).
Next, the phrase "practicing according to reality" and so forth is a formal praise of the virtue of practice.
According to the *Ratnagotravibhāga*,
in terms of the wisdom of the fundamental nature (*mūla-jñāna*), it is called "practice according to reality" (*yathāvadbhāvikā*);
its subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) is called "universal engagement" (*sarvatragā*).
The phrase "practicing according to reality" mentioned here refers to the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*).
The subsequent mention of "and so forth" [refers to the subsequently attained wisdom].
One takes up the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*). According to the *Dharmasaṃgīti-sūtra*,
this encompasses the beginning and end of all practices.
These are subsumed under two categories:
namely, practicing according to reality and heedfulness.
As that sutra says: "One who practices according to reality" refers to one who has generated the aspiration for enlightenment (bodhicitta).
Heedfulness means fulfilling the vow for enlightenment.
Furthermore, it is the practice according to reality.
That is to say, one practices generosity; as for being heedful,
it means not seeking a reward.
Thus maintaining pure precepts,
they achieve non-retrogression;
or they cultivate the practice of patience.
They attain the patience of non-arising;
they seek all roots of goodness without weariness;
and they relinquish all conditioned activities.
He cultivates meditative concentration without dwelling in meditative concentration;
he fulfills wisdom without engaging in conceptual proliferation regarding all phenomena,
in that respective order.
"Practicing according to reality and being heedful," and so forth,
as explained at length.
Now, regarding the phrase "practicing according to reality":
This includes the arousal of the aspiration for enlightenment up until the fulfillment of wisdom.
Next, the word "etcetera" (ādi) refers to the inclusion of heedfulness (apramāda).
This is precisely the fulfillment of the bodhicitta vow,
up to and including the non-conceptualization of all phenomena.
The homage to the Triple Gem has already been completed above.
The following verse describes the general intent of composing this treatise.
This general intent does not exceed two aspects:
the first half clarifies that [the purpose] is to transform sentient beings below.
The second half of the passage reveals the supreme propagation of the Buddha-way.
The reason sentient beings remain perpetually submerged in the ocean of birth and death and do not proceed toward the shore of nirvana is solely due to doubt and false attachments.
Therefore, the essential method for now transforming sentient beings below is to cause them to eliminate doubt and abandon false attachments.
To discuss doubt in general terms:
There are many such paths.
Those who seek the Mahāyāna have two kinds of doubts:
the first is doubt regarding the Dharma.
The first obstructs the arousal of the mind;
the second is the gate of doubt,
which obstructs spiritual practice.
Regarding what is called "doubting the Dharma," it refers to raising this doubt:
"Is the essence of the Mahāyāna Dharma one or many? Thus, it is one.
Then there would be no distinct phenomena.
Because there are no distinct phenomena,
there would be no sentient beings.
For whom does the Bodhisattva give rise to the great vow?
If there were many dharmas,
they would not be of one essence.
Because they are not of one essence,
things and the self are each distinct;
how, then, can the great compassion of same-essence arise?
Due to such doubt, one is unable to resolve the mind [for awakening].
Regarding what is called the "gate of doubt":
The gates of the teaching established by the Tathāgata are numerous.
Upon which gate should one rely to first initiate practice?
If there is one that may be relied upon by all, [what is it?]
One cannot enter [the path] all at once.
If one relies on [only] one or two [aspects],
what would be discarded and what would be pursued?
Because of these doubts,
one is unable to initiate spiritual practice;
therefore, I shall now dispel these two kinds of doubt.
Establishing the dharma of the one mind,
two gates are opened.
Regarding the establishment of the dharma of the one mind:
This dispels the initial doubt,
clarifying that the Mahāyāna Dharma consists solely of the one mind;
apart from this one mind, there are no other dharmas whatsoever.
It is only because of ignorance that one’s own single mind becomes deluded,
giving rise to various waves that circulate through the six realms of existence.
Although these waves of the six realms arise, [the nature of the mind remains unchanged].
One does not depart from the ocean of the single mind;
for it is precisely because the single mind gives rise to the six realms that one is able to give rise to the vow of great salvation.
The six realms do not transcend the single mind;
therefore, one can give rise to great compassion of identical essence.
In this way, doubts are dispelled.
Thus one attains the arousal of the great mind (*mahācitta*).
Regarding the opening of the two gates,
this dispels the second doubt.
Although the various teaching gates are numerous,
the initial entry into practice does not transcend two doors:
one relies on the gate of True Suchness (tathatā) to cultivate the practice of tranquility (śamatha).
Based on the gate of arising and ceasing, one initiates contemplative practice;
with the dual cultivation of śamatha and vipaśyanā,
all myriad practices are fully perfected.

Regarding the statement that within the evolving consciousnesses one relies on the moving mind to perceive appearances:
this means that based on the movement of the preceding karmic consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*),
it evolves into the appearance of the perceiving subject.
However, there are two aspects to the evolving consciousness (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*). If it is that which, being moved by ignorance, evolves to become the seer,
this resides within the fundamental consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*).
When that which is moved and transformed by its objects becomes the seer,
this is called the seven consciousnesses;
herein lies the aspect of transformation.
This refers to the first meaning.
Regarding the statement that the manifesting consciousness (ādarśa-vijñāna) can manifest all objective realms,
this is based on the perceiving aspect (darśana-bhāga) of the aforementioned evolving consciousnesses (pravṛtti-vijñāna).
Furthermore, it gives rise to the function of manifestation.
As stated above, "because one relies on the capacity for seeing, objects falsely appear.
One should know that the manifesting consciousness (nirbhāsa-vijñāna) relies upon the evolving consciousness (pravṛtti-vijñāna).
The function of seeing is not itself the function of manifesting;
therefore, what was previously stated as "capable of seeing" and "capable of manifesting" is followed by an analogy.
The subsequent section on "correspondence" (he) mentions the five sense objects (*pañca-viṣaya*).
This refers to the coarse and manifest aspects, cited here to correspond with physical forms and images (*rūpa*).
This is because the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states that it "pervades and manifests all objects" and "arises spontaneously at all times,
always remaining present," unlike the sixth and seventh consciousnesses, which are occasionally interrupted and cease.
Based on this textual evidence,
one should know that these three are all distinct functions existing within the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*).
As for the fourth, the wisdom-consciousness (*jñānavijñāna*):
This is the first of the six aspects within the seventh consciousness, namely the aspect of cognition (*jñāna-lakṣaṇa*);
its meaning is as previously explained. It refers to the fruits of the desirable and the undesirable.
These are called defiled and pure phenomena.
One discriminates those phenomena and conceives of them as "I" and "mine."
Therefore, it is said that this refers to the discrimination of defiled and pure phenomena.
As for the fifth, the "continuing consciousness," it is precisely what is called the "continuing characteristic" among the six characteristics of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
Regarding "because it is not severed due to its association with mindfulness": this refers to the association with the grasping at phenomena (*dharmagrāha*),
which results in a long-lasting continuity.
This explains the meaning of "continuity" (saṃtati) by way of the non-interruption of its own essence.
From "maintaining" (sthiti-dhāraṇa) onwards,
it explains the meaning of continuity by way of its functional capacity.
This consciousness can give rise to the afflictions of craving and grasping;
thus, it can draw forth and sustain the various formations (*saṃskāra*) produced by past ignorance,
enabling them to become "existence" (*bhava*) capable of producing future fruits.
Therefore, it is said that they "maintain" [existence] up until the point of not losing it.
Furthermore, they can give rise to the afflictions that moisten rebirth,
enabling the continuity of karmic results to proceed without interruption.
Therefore, it is said that this is accomplished because there is no discrepancy.
Thus, the continuous flow of cause and effect throughout the three periods of time depends upon the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
For this reason, it is called the "continuing consciousness" (*saṃtati-vijñāna*).
Next, the statement that it "recalls past events and anticipates future events" reveals that the function of this consciousness is coarse and manifest discernment.
This subtle discrimination of differing cognitions is known to exist only within the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*),
and is not the same as the continuous mind described above.
From here on, the third section concludes by clarifying the meaning of relying upon the mind.
This section contains two parts.
First, it is brief;
later, it is detailed.
Regarding the initial phrase "therefore":
The five kinds of consciousness and so forth previously mentioned are established based upon the mind.
For this reason, all phenomena within the three realms are created solely by the mind.
As the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* states:
"O Son of the Buddha,
the three realms are produced by the mind alone."
This is what is meant by that.
How this meaning is explained is set forth in detail below;
therein are two parts.
First, it is clarified that all phenomena are not non-existent, yet they are not existent.
Second, it is revealed that all phenomena are not existent, yet they are not entirely non-existent.
Regarding the first point, it is stated that "all phenomena arise from the mind and are produced by deluded thought."
This clarifies that all phenomena are not without manifestation.

The statement that "all discrimination is the discrimination of one's own mind; the mind does not see the mind, for there is no characteristic to be found" clarifies the meaning that all phenomena are not existent.
As stated in the ten-fascicle sutra:
"The body, the means of subsistence,
and the environment— if they arise like a dream,"
There should be two kinds of mind,
yet the mind has no dual characteristics;
it is like a blade that cannot cut itself.
A finger cannot point to itself,
just as the mind cannot see itself;
the matter is likewise so.
The commentary states:
If the various things seen within a dream were real existents in the manner they are perceived, [then...]
Thus, there appear the two aspects of the seer and the seen;
yet, within that dream, these two phenomena do not truly exist.
All minds within the three realms are just like this dream.
Apart from the mind, there is nothing that can be discriminated;
therefore, it is said that all discrimination is the discrimination of one's own mind.
Yet, this very mind cannot see itself.
Just as with a sword or a finger,
it is said that the mind does not see the mind;
since there is nothing else to be seen, [the mind cannot perceive itself].
Nor can it see itself; because that which is seen does not exist,
that which sees does not exist.
Since both the subjective and objective aspects are non-apprehendable,
it is said that no characteristic can be apprehended. Herein,
the difficulties are resolved and the views of the New and Old [schools] are harmonized.
This is as explained in the separate record regarding the analysis of atoms (*paramāṇu*).
One should know that from here below,
the meaning of being neither existent nor non-existent is clarified.
The initial statement, "One should know that from the world up to its lack of substantiality, nothing can be apprehended,
for it is but the delusion of mind," clarifies non-existence.
The subsequent passage, beginning with "Because the mind arises, phenomena arise," and so forth, [clarifies dependent origination].
This demonstrates that it is not non-existent;
by the power of ignorance, the mind moves without awareness,
even to the point of manifesting all objective realms and so forth.
Therefore it is said that when the mind arises, all manner of phenomena arise;
if the mind of ignorance ceases, its objects likewise cease,
and all discriminative consciousnesses are completely extinguished.
Therefore, it is said that when the mind ceases, the various phenomena cease;
this does not clarify arising and ceasing in terms of momentary succession.
The detailed explanation of the underlying meaning is now complete.
Next, the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is explained.
Mental consciousness is precisely the previously mentioned continuous consciousness;
however, it is distinguished here from the perspective of its arising in association with the conceptualization of grasping at phenomena (*dharmagrāha-vikalpa*).
It is designated as "mind" (manas);
however, with respect to its capacity to give rise to the afflictions of views and craving from the gateway of prior birth,
it is called "mental consciousness" (mano-vijñāna).
Therefore, what is called "mental consciousness" (manovijñāna) is precisely this continuity;
up to the point where it discriminates the six sense objects, it is termed mental consciousness.
This treatise addresses the meaning of this single mental consciousness.
Therefore, the five consciousnesses, such as the visual consciousness, are not treated separately.
Thus it is said that the mental consciousness discriminates the six sense objects;
it is also called the "discriminating consciousness" (vibhāga-vijñāna).
It separately apprehends the six sense objects based upon the six sense faculties;
it is not like the manas, which does not depend on distinct faculties,
and is therefore called "separated."
Furthermore, because it can discern various phenomena and characteristics regarding the past, the future, the internal, and the external,
it is also called the "discriminative consciousness of phenomena" (*vastu-vijñapti-vijñāna*).
This is because it functions through the sense of increasing the afflictions of views and craving.
This explains the meaning of the *vicitra-vastu-vijñāna* (the consciousness of various objects).
Because it is augmented by the afflictions of the paths of seeing and cultivation,
it is able to differentiate various kinds of phenomena.
The characteristics of the six superior [aggregates]—namely, the internal aggregates of feeling, perception, and formations—are subsumed within this consciousness.
The preceding section has extensively elucidated the meaning of arising and ceasing as dependent upon causes and conditions;
hereafter follows the second part, which further clarifies the essential nature and characteristics of that which serves as the basis for those causes and conditions.
Within this, there are two parts:
first, a brief clarification of the profundity of causes and conditions;
second, an extensive manifestation of the distinctions among causes and conditions.
The beginning and middle have three parts:
first, the indication of its profundity;
second, the explanation.
The subsequent section provides the conclusion. Regarding the initial statement,

"the consciousness arising from the perfuming of ignorance," this restates what was previously explained concerning the basis of the *ālayavijñāna*, namely that it arises through the non-awakening of ignorance.
"That none other can know it, but only a Buddha thoroughly understands it" marks its profundity.
As for the section beginning with "Why is this so?"...
Next, the profound meaning is explained:
"That which has been intrinsically pure from the very beginning yet is defiled by ignorance, and thus possesses a defiled mind," means that while it is luminous and pure, it is perpetually defiled.
Although there is a defiled mind, it remains constant and unchanging;
this clarifies that while there is movement, there is always stillness.
It is by virtue of this principle.
It is profoundly deep and difficult to fathom.
As stated in the *Bhāryāsūtra*:
"The intrinsically pure mind."
It is difficult to comprehend;
that mind, being defiled by afflictions,
is likewise difficult to comprehend.
The *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states:
"Because the Tathāgatagarbha is by nature pure,
it is defiled by adventitious afflictions and impurities."
Based on this meaning,
for the sake of Queen Śrīmālā and other bodhisattvas,
I have taught that the tathāgatagarbha and the ālayavijñāna arise together with the seven consciousnesses.
This is called the characteristic of transformation and cessation, Mahāmati.
It is the realm of the Tathāgatagarbha and the Ālayavijñāna.
I now, together with you and all the bodhisattvas who possess profound wisdom,
am able to discern and distinguish these two kinds of dharmas;
whereas other śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and followers of external paths remain attached to mere names.
"Being unable to fully comprehend these two dharmas,
this meaning can be known only by the Buddha"—
this is the third summary of profundity.
The so-called "second section" below extensively elucidates the distinctions among causes and conditions.
Within this, there are six parts;
the first clarifies the essential nature and characteristics of the cause of the mind's essence.
First, it reveals the essential nature and characteristics of ignorance as a condition;
second, it clarifies the distinctions among the various conditions for the defiled mind;
third, it reveals the stages and levels at which ignorance is treated and severed.
Fifth, the explanation of the meanings of association and non-association.
Sixth, the discernment of the meanings of cognitive obstruction and afflictive obstruction.
Regarding the first of these, it is said that because the nature of the mind is eternally free from discursive thought, it is called "unchanging."
The preceding passage explains the meaning of how the mind, though possessed of defiled thoughts, remains eternally unchanging;
and though its entire substance is in motion, it is fundamentally quiescent.
Therefore, it is said that the nature of the mind is eternally free from discursive thought.
Regarding the phrase "not associated with the mind" (*cittaviprayukta*) in the second [category],
it clarifies that this ignorance is extremely subtle,
such that there is yet no differentiation between subject and object, nor between primary and secondary mental factors.
Therefore, it is said that they are dissociated from the mind;
this alone is the fundamental basis.
There is no other defiled dharma more subtle than this that could exist prior to it.
For this reason, it is said that [the afflictions] arise suddenly.
As the *Mūlakarma-sūtra* states:
"Prior to the four stages of abiding (catur-vāsabhūmi), no further dharmas arise."
Therefore, it is called the "ground of beginningless ignorance" (*anādikālikā-avidyā-vāsabhūmi*).
This clarifies that there is nothing else preceding it to serve as a beginning;
this alone is the root.
Therefore, it is said that there is no beginning;
this is precisely the meaning of "sudden" (*akasmāt*) in this treatise.
This is explained as being "without predecessor" (*apūrva*) by way of the gate of mutual dependence between the subtle and the coarse.
It is also said that it "suddenly arises.
This "sudden arising" of the characteristic of ignorance is not spoken of in reference to temporal duration.
This is as extensively analyzed in the chapter on the two obstructions (*dvividhāvaraṇa*).
It explains the preceding statement: "Though its intrinsic nature is pure, it is defiled by ignorance; thus there is a mind that is defiled."
Within this, there are two parts:
a general heading and a detailed explanation.
Within the detailed explanation,
the remedies and the abandonments are also revealed;
herein lie the six defilements.
This refers to the aforementioned mental consciousness along with the five types of mental consciousness;
however, because the preceding section clarified the meaning of arising based on causes,
they were explained in order from the subtle to the coarse.
Now, because I wish to simultaneously clarify the stages of cultivation and severance,
I shall explain the sequence from the coarse to the subtle.
First is the defilement associated with grasping (*saṃprayukta-kleśa*).
This refers to the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*),
in the sense that it is augmented by the afflictions of view and craving,
and because it is associated with coarse discrimination and grasping.
If persons of the two vehicles reach the stage of Arhat,
they have attained ultimate detachment from the afflictions of both the path of seeing and the path of cultivation;
as for Bodhisattvas, however—
Because those at the stage of ten understandings (daśa-avabodha) and above are able to remain far removed [from such faults].
This reference to the "stage associated with faith" (adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi) pertains to the level of the ten understandings.
When the faculty of faith is accomplished and there is no regression or loss,
it is called "conjoined with faith."
As stated in the *Benevolent Kings Sūtra*:
"The thirty individuals of the noble embryo of the patience of subduing consist of the ten stages of faith,
the ten stages of cessation, and the ten stages of firm resolve."
It should be understood that herein, the ten stages of Dedication (daśa-pratipatti) are called "firmness" (dṛḍha);
the ten stages of Practice (daśa-caryā) are called "cessation" (śama); and the ten stages of Faith-Understanding (daśa-adhimukti) are called "faith" (śraddhā).
Upon entering this stage, one has already realized the emptiness of persons; thus,
the afflictions of both the path of seeing and the path of cultivation can no longer manifest.
Therefore, it is called "detachment.
One should know that what is elucidated throughout this treatise,
from beginning to end, explains the antidotes and abandonments in terms of their actual manifestation.
The second, the defilement associated with non-interruption,
refers to the continuous consciousness within the five kinds of mind,
which arises in succession in association with the grasping of dharmas.
"Non-interruption" is another name for "continuity.

From the stage of the ten levels of understanding (*daśa-adhimukti*), one cultivates the contemplation of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātratā*) through the skillful means of thorough investigation (*paryeṣaṇā*).
Up to the first bhūmi, one realizes the three natures of non-substantiality;
thus, the conceptualization of grasping at phenomena (*dharmagrāha-vikalpa*) can no longer manifest.
Therefore, it is said that the "Pure Mind-ground" is attained because of ultimate detachment.
The third, the defilement associated with the discerning cognition (*vikalpa-jñāna*),
refers to the fourth consciousness, the mental consciousness (*mano-vijñāna*), among the five types of mind;
it persists up through the seventh stage (*bhūmi*).
When the two types of knowledge arise,
they cannot manifest; one must emerge from contemplation to engage with external objects.
Since they can also manifest during the state of spontaneous mental activity,
it is said that one gradually departs from them.
From the seventh bhūmi upward, one enters meditative observation for long durations;
therefore, this manas never manifests again.
Hence it is said that it is ultimately abandoned in the stage of the skillful means of signlessness.
This seventh stage involves applied effort and deliberate exertion within the contemplation of signlessness; therefore,
it is called the Stage of Skillful Means regarding Signlessness.
The fourth is the defilement of the manifestation of forms that is non-associated [with thought].
Among the five kinds of mind, it is the third, the manifesting consciousness (nirvikalpa-manovijñāna),
which is like the appearance of reflected images within a clear mirror.
Therefore, it is called the "stain of non-correspondence with manifested form.
This is the stage of mastery over form;
it is the eighth stage.
Having already attained mastery over the pure land (*śuddhakṣetra*),
coarse forms of the defiled land (*saṃkliṣṭakṣetra*) cannot appear; therefore,
it is said that one is able to leave them behind.
The five [factors] such as "seeing" that are defiled and dissociated from mind are the second transformation-consciousness within the manas;
they constitute the capacity for seeing by depending upon the moving mind.
The Stage of Mastery over the Mind is the ninth stage. On this stage,
one has already attained the four types of unimpeded knowledge (*pratisaṃvid*).
Because that which possesses obstruction cannot arise as an object of cognition,
it is said to be "able to be separated from.
Regarding the sixth fundamental defilement, non-concomitance with karma:
Among these five aspects of mind, the first is the karmic consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*).
Because it moves due to the power of ignorance and fails to realize [the nature of] the mind,
those Bodhisattvas who have reached the final stage [of the ten bhūmis]...
This is the tenth stage;
since its Stainless Stage (vimalā-bhūmi) belongs to this very stage,
speaking from the perspective of ultimate reality:
In the tenth stage (*bhūmi*), there are likewise subtle aspects of transformation and manifestation; however,
they are said to be gradually abandoned according to the characteristics of each respective stage,
as stated in the passage below.
Based upon the karmic consciousness,
up to and including the ultimate stage of a Bodhisattva,
that which is perceived by the mind [is as follows].
This is called the Reward Body (*saṃbhogakāya*).
If one is separated from the karmic consciousness (*karmavijñāna*), then the characteristic of seeing does not exist.
One should know that as long as the karmic consciousness (*karma-vijñāna*) has not been exhausted,
the capacity to perceive and manifest will likewise not be exhausted.
The following section, the fourth, clarifies the cessation through the realization of non-existence.
However, the ground of abiding ignorance has two meanings.
If one discusses it in terms of the gate of abiding through active functioning,
it can be gradually severed from the first bhūmi upward.
If one approaches this from the perspective of the gate of abiding in the stages through birth,
it can be severed only by the wisdom of a Buddha’s bodhi;
in this treatise, we do not differentiate between birth and activity.
Taken together, these two are collectively termed "ignorance" (*avidyā*). Therefore,
it is said that upon entering the Stage of the Pure Mind (*śuddhacittabhūmi*), one attains detachment according to one's capacity,
continuing until the Stage of the Tathāgata, where one is able to achieve ultimate detachment.
Below this, the fifth section clarifies the meaning of association (*saṃprayoga*) and non-association (*asaṃprayoga*).
Among the six types of defilements (*kleśa*), the first three are associated.
The latter three defilements and ignorance are dissociated.
Regarding the statement in the section on association that "mind and mental factors are distinct," this is a designation for mental phenomena (*caitta*).
In the *Kātyāyanīputra-śāstra*,
these are termed "mind" (*citta*) and "mental factors" (*caitasika-dharma*).
Regarding their distinction based on defilement and purity:
It refers to the distinctions among various phenomena—defiled and pure—such as views, pride, craving, and so forth. Regarding "knowing that which has the same characteristic":
it means being able to know that which possesses the same characteristic.
"Having the same object-condition" means having the same focal object (*ālambana*). Here,
"association" (*samprayoga*) is explained by way of three meanings.
This means that the distinctness of mental states and mental objects refers to their identity in essence;
that is to say, each of the various categories of afflictions possesses a single essence.
Because there is no second [factor] in either case,
that which knows the same characteristic is the meaning of "knowing equally," and that which takes the same characteristic as its object is the meaning of "taking equally as an object."
Those first three defilements possess these three characteristics and exist simultaneously.
Therefore, it is called "conjunction" (saṃprayoga).
Question:
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states:
All primary minds and mental factors have the same object of cognition,
but not the same mode of apprehension.
They exist simultaneously,
yet each functions individually; here,
the explanation regarding the characteristics of cognition is likewise the same.
Since these are thus contradictory,
how are they to be reconciled? Answer:
Both meanings exist;
therefore, they are not contradictory. Why is this?
Just as I see this practice of the nature of seeing,
so too do those who possess self-love practice the nature of self-love;
such are the differences in their practices.
Although their names differ and they belong to different categories,
views (*dṛṣṭi*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), and so forth all function as the conception of a self (*ātma-grāha*).
Based on this meaning, it is said that they are "identical in their mode of cognition" (*jñāna-samāna*).
Therefore, these two explanations do not contradict one another.

Regarding the statement within the section on "Non-correspondence" that "the mind itself is unaware and is eternally without distinction," this clarifies the meaning of being without intrinsic substance and so forth.
Because there are no distinct numerical categories apart from the mind,
and since they lack intrinsic nature and so forth,
these meanings do not exist apart from the mind.
As for the remaining two [factors], upon what could they rely?
Therefore, there is no sense of knowing together or sharing the same object-condition (*ālambana*).
Thus it is said that they do not know each other or condition each other as characteristics.
In this context, "not" means "non-existent.
Question:
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states that the ālayavijñāna is associated with five mental factors.
It takes two kinds of objects;
namely, the manifest form and the non-associated defilements within this treatise.
For what reason is it called "non-associated" here?
Answer: The intent of this treatise is to explain the meaning of the transformation [of the mind] according to the distinctions in the number of afflictions.
It is called "associated.
Within the manifesting consciousness (*nirbhāsa-vijñāna*),
there are no afflictions (*kleśa*).
Based on this meaning,
it is called "non-associated";
such is the intention of that new treatise.
It is said to be associated based on the enumeration of universal factors;
it is by this principle that [this is stated].
Nor is there any contradiction.
Below this, the sixth section clarifies the meaning of the two obstructions;
in the "Gate of Manifestation," they are termed the two hindrances (*āvaraṇa*).
Within the hidden gate (guhyamukha), these are termed the two obstructions (dvayāvaraṇa).
This meaning is explained in full detail in the chapter on the two hindrances (dvayāvaraṇa-pariccheda).
In the present passage, however, the hidden gate is discussed.
Within this, there are two parts.
The first part divides [the subject] into two obstructions;
the following explains this meaning.
To explain the reason for this:
regarding the meaning of "defiled mind" mentioned at the beginning,
it serves to reveal the six types of defiled minds.
Fundamental wisdom is the wisdom that illuminates quiescence;
it is so called because it accords with tranquility.
This is called the hindrance of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*).
As for the meaning of ignorance (*avidyā*), it refers to fundamental ignorance (*mūlāvidyā*).
The knowledge of worldly activities is subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*).
Ignorance is deluded confusion, devoid of any discrimination.
Therefore, it contradicts the discriminative cognition of the world;
based on this meaning, it is called an obstruction to knowledge (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
The commentary explains the reason for this:
it precisely clarifies this meaning—
that based on the defiled mind, one is able to see and manifest, thereby falsely grasping at objects.

To briefly enumerate them: the evolving consciousness (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*), the manifesting consciousness (*darśana-vijñāna*), and the cognitive consciousness (*jñāna-vijñāna*). These contravene the nature of equality;
that is, they contravene the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) in which subject and object are equal.
This explains the meaning of the obstruction of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*).

The statement that "all phenomena are eternally quiescent and devoid of the characteristic of arising" refers to the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) as it is deludedly perceived by ignorance (*avidyā*).
"Because ignorance is non-awakening and thus falsely opposes the Dharma" clarifies that ignorance is deluded regarding the meaning of the dharmatā. Therefore,
it cannot attain even the slightest knowledge.
This clearly explains the meaning of how [the nature of reality] contradicts worldly cognition.
The second section, the extensive explanation of the causes and conditions of arising and ceasing, is hereby concluded.
This marks the end of the first fascicle of the *Commentary on the Awakening of Faith*.
*Commentary on the Treatise on the Awakening of Faith*, Scroll II.
Furthermore, the following third section extensively explains the characteristics of arising and ceasing (*utpāda-nirodha*) from the "Section on Establishing the Meaning" (*lìyìfēn*).
This section contains two parts: first, it clarifies the coarse and subtle characteristics of arising and ceasing; second, it reveals the coarse and subtle aspects of arising and ceasing.
Regarding this meaning,
there are also two parts in the beginning and middle.
The first is the explicit clarification of the coarse and the subtle.
Second is the classification according to persons.
This also has two parts at the beginning:
a general heading.
Another interpretation:
regarding the statement in the section on "another interpretation" that "the first [affliction] is coarse because it is associated with the mind," among the six types of defilements:
The first three defilements are associated with the mind;
their characteristics are coarse and manifest.
The Sūtra states that these are called "arising and ceasing.
As for the second point, "because they are subtle and do not associate with the mind," this refers to the latter three defiled minds.
This is dissociated [from mind];
it lacks the coarse and manifest characteristics of mind and mental factors,
for its essence is subtle.
It flows constantly without interruption.
In the sutras, this is called "successive arising and ceasing.
As the Ten-Scroll Sutra says:
There are two kinds of cessation of consciousness. What are the two?
The first is the cessation of characteristics.
Second, the cessation of the continuity [of the aggregates].
Birth and abiding are also like this.
As the four-fascicle *Sūtra* says:
All consciousnesses have two kinds of arising, abiding, and ceasing:
namely, the arising of the continuous flow (*pravāha*) and the arising of the manifestation (*nimitta*).
Cessation is likewise twofold.
In the Sūtra, only the names of these two types are directly stated without their characteristics being specifically revealed; therefore,
the author of this treatise now examines them according to the meaning of association and non-association.
This is to distinguish between the two types of coarse and subtle characteristics.
Within the analysis according to persons,
that which is the coarsest among the coarse is as follows:
This refers to the first two among the aforementioned three.
That which is subtle within the coarse refers to the last one among these three.
Previously, the first two [stages] both occurred within the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
Because their modes of activity (*ākāra*) were coarse,
they were known by ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*).
The first [of the three periods]— past, present, and future— is the seventh consciousness;
its mode of activity is not coarse and is not perceived by ordinary beings.
In the latter [section], the first two [verses] show that the subject and object are distinct in their capacities for manifesting and perceiving; therefore,
these are what is known by the Bodhisattva.
As for the last one, because the subject and object have not yet been differentiated,
only a Buddha can fully comprehend it.
Below this, the second section clarifies the meaning of arising and ceasing.
Within it, there are two parts.
First, the conditions for arising are clarified.
This subsequently clarifies the meaning of cessation.
Within the first [section], there are also two parts.
First, it explains the universal object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
To subsequently clarify the specific causes:
